Second-stage bioassay pre-training · 5×5 cross validation · two data sets

What a PCBA stage buys a 3D encoder

Atom-JEPA-Bio1 continues the released Atom-JEPA encoder2 with a second pre-training stage that adds a supervised loss over 1,089 PCBA bioassays3 to its self-supervised objectives, and fine-tunes it on ADMET exactly as before. Its authors scored it on this site's protocol and report it best or tied on 34 of 45 endpoint × metric combinations, against 18 for Monroe + TabPFN 34. Run here with their code and weights, on the same folds, the count comes out at 35 against 17. Only the checkpoint differs from the Atom-JEPA study, so the bioassay stage can be measured directly: fine-tuned, it is ahead of stage 1 on 32 of the 45 paired calls and behind on one. On Biogen it turns a deficit against Monroe into a lead: stage 1 was behind on 13 of 18 combinations, Bio is ahead on 12.

7methods compared
15endpoints
5×5cross validation

27GPU hours

One checkpoint swapped

The fine-tuned arm is the authors' train_multitask from github.com/khelverskovp/atom-jepa at commit 64d539b, whose fine-tuning configuration is identical to the commit the stage-1 study ran. It reads the bio encoder from the Hugging Face Hub in place of molecules, and nothing else changes: one multitask model per fold, the encoder frozen for ten of fifty epochs, ten RDKit conformers per molecule — the very conformer files the stage-1 study used — and the test prediction averaged over all ten. The best epoch is picked on the held-out fifth of the training set and every arm is scored on the same untouched test set.

Two frozen arms read the stage-1 and the Bio encoder, eight layers mean-pooled, through the TabPFN 35 call the Monroe arm makes; both are fitted here, on the same machine. LightGBM on Morgan counts6, ChemProp fine-tuned from CheMeleon7 and Monroe + TabPFN 3 are imported from the nine-method foundation-model comparison, and stage-1 Atom-JEPA fine-tuned from the Atom-JEPA study, none of them re-run.

The authors' tables compare six arms — the stage-1 frozen arm is not among them — and import the comparators' per-fold results from this site, as this study does. The count is within one of theirs: 35 of 45 for fine-tuned Bio against their 34, 17 for Monroe against their 18. The fine-tuned folds here are a separate training of the same recipe, not the authors' fold models, so an exact match was not to be expected; the comparators' folds are the same in both.

The bioassay stage, measured

Paired by fold, fine-tuned Bio against fine-tuned stage-1 Atom-JEPA is ahead on three of the 9 endpoints on all three metrics and split on the other six (14 ahead and 1 behind of 27 endpoint × metric combinations) on ExpansionRx and ahead on all six endpoints on all three metrics (18 of 18 endpoint × metric combinations) on Biogen. The loss is LOG_MGMB MAE on ExpansionRx, by 0.0045 with 9 of 25 folds better, one of the pair's 45 uncorrected tests. It raises mean R² on 14 of 15 endpoints, by a median +0.024 on ExpansionRx and +0.067 on Biogen. Frozen and read by TabPFN 3 the stage does more: the Bio embedding is ahead of the stage-1 one on 37 of 45 combinations and behind on two, a median +0.057 R² on ExpansionRx and +0.109 on Biogen, and better on 13 of 15 endpoints.

Not the machine

Stage-1 Atom-JEPA was fine-tuned for the earlier study on an RTX 5070 Ti and a DGX Spark, and every Bio fold on Biogen on an RTX PRO 5000. To see how far a change of machine moves the same recipe on its own, the stage-1 arm was re-trained here on the 5 folds of Biogen's first repeat. The re-run lands within 0.007 R² of the imported folds on every endpoint; Bio is at least 0.039 above them on every endpoint.

Against Monroe

Fine-tuned Bio is ahead on six and behind on one of the 9 endpoints on all three metrics and split on the other two (18 ahead and 7 behind of 27 endpoint × metric combinations) on ExpansionRx, and ahead on three and behind on one of the 6 endpoints on all three metrics and split on the other two (12 ahead and 3 behind of 18 endpoint × metric combinations) on Biogen. Stage-1 Atom-JEPA, against the same Monroe folds, had been 18 ahead and 9 behind on ExpansionRx and 3 ahead and 13 behind on Biogen. Frozen, the Bio embedding is ahead of Monroe's on Biogen (11 ahead, 4 behind) and behind it on ExpansionRx (4 ahead, 17 behind); fine-tuning is still what wins, ahead of the frozen Bio arm on 35 of 45 paired calls and behind on five.

Where it still loses is where stage 1 lost. On ExpansionRx it is behind Monroe on every metric of LOG_MLM, on Biogen on LOG_MDR1_ER, and on some metrics of LOG_Caco_AB and LOG_Caco_Efflux. Caco-2 A→B remains Monroe's: an R² of 0.471 ± 0.041 over the 25 folds against 0.279 ± 0.185 for fine-tuned Bio and 0.103 ± 0.219 for stage 1. Across the fifteen endpoints, the rank correlation between molecules per training fold and Bio's margin over Monroe is −0.09.

Was it pre-trained on the test set?

Stage 2 trains on PCBA as Monroe's pipeline prepares it, which moves the test splits of the public benchmarks out of training — but those are the Polaris splits of the Biogen data, not this site's. Matching every test molecule to the PCBA table by standard InChI, Monroe's own deduplication key, finds 162 of Biogen's 1,058 test molecules (15%) and none of ExpansionRx's 2,282. That is an upper bound on what reached training. The assays are rarely ADMET: one solubility assay, AID 1996, labels 12 of the matched Biogen molecules. Monroe's pre-training draws on the same table, so any exposure is shared by the arm Bio is compared with.

On the molecules PCBA does not have, fine-tuned Bio is still below stage 1 in MAE on all six endpoints and below Monroe on LOG_HLM, LOG_HPPB, LOG_RLM and LOG_SOL. The molecules PCBA has are harder, not easier: Monroe's MAE is higher on them on all six endpoints. The gain does not come from having seen the test set.

What it costs

The recipe is unchanged, and so is the cost: a median 62 minutes per ExpansionRx fold on the RTX 5070 Ti against 59 for stage 1 on the same card. The Bio folds ran on two machines, 37 on an RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell and 13 on an RTX 5070 Ti, each fold from its own seed, with the claimed folds of each machine skipped by the other.

What this does and does not say

Scope

One recipe. The fine-tuning hyperparameters are the authors' and are used unchanged on both data sets, as in the stage-1 study. Nothing is tuned for Monroe either.

Conformers are pinned. RDKit's conformer generator does not give the same conformers across releases even with a fixed seed: a newer RDKit changed them for about a third of the Biogen molecules, and that alone moved the frozen stage-1 arm by up to 0.10 R² on the plasma-binding endpoints. Every Atom-JEPA arm here reads the stage-1 study's conformer files, checked by hash.

An upper bound on exposure. The PCBA match is by structure, before the authors' hold-out of the benchmark test splits, which could not be reproduced here. The real overlap with what stage 2 trained on is at most what is reported.

Reported the way “Even More Thoughts on ML Method Comparisons” and the protocol paper it points at10 argue comparisons should be: distributions over folds, simultaneous confidence intervals, paired tests on the folds, and no bolded maxima. A win or a loss in the paired tables is a t-test at p < 0.05 on one endpoint and one metric, uncorrected.

Code, per-fold metrics and every figure: studies/atom-jepa-bio.
